Reading the Tide Tables

A tide table is a promise made by arithmetic. Twice a day the sea withdraws from the harbour mouth and twice a day it returns, and the times of those turnings can be computed years in advance from the motions of the moon and sun. The harbourmaster's almanac prints them in columns: high water, low water, and the height of each in metres above chart datum.

The rule of twelfths is the sailor's shortcut for everything the table leaves out. In the first hour after low water the tide rises by one twelfth of its range; in the second, two twelfths; then three, three, two, and one again — a bell curve you can hold in your head while the boat dries out beneath you and the mud begins to glisten.

Spring tides arrive just after the new and full moons, when sun and moon pull together and the range is at its greatest; neap tides follow the quarter moons, lazy and shallow. The difference matters in a drying harbour, where a spring ebb can leave a yacht sitting in the mud a full hour earlier than the same clock time a week later.

None of this arithmetic survives contact with the weather unchanged. A hard onshore wind can hold a tide in the harbour long past its printed time, and a falling barometer can lift the sea by a hand's breadth before a single cloud shows. The old pilots read the tables the way musicians read a score: as the shape of the thing, not the thing itself.
